meta.title: Activity-based management and ABC beyond the factory
meta.summary: Using ABC for pricing and product mix, cost reduction and value-added analysis, design decisions, ABC in merchandising and services, time-driven ABC, and activity-based budgeting.

videos.title: Using ABC for pricing and mix
videos.take: Activity-based management uses ABC information to make better pricing, mix and process decisions

scenes.say: ABC is only worth building if managers use it. Using activity information to run the business is called activity-based management.
Activity-based management, or A-B-M, is the use of activity cost information to make decisions: about prices, product mix, cost reduction, process improvement and design.

scenes.heading: Prairie Gate's lines under ABC
scenes.say: With ABC costs, utility trailers sell for $9,200 and cost $8,700, a $500 margin. Livestock trailers sell for $16,400 but cost $18,280: each one loses $1,880. The old system showed them as Prairie Gate's most profitable line.

scenes.heading: Options for the livestock line
items: Raise prices or charge for custom design
Cut the cost of design and setups
scenes.say: Karen has options: raise livestock prices or charge separately for custom design; cut the cost of the activities the line uses; or, at the extreme, drop it.

sub: if the line goes: Cost II, Lecture 7
scenes.say: Dropping a line is rarely the first answer. Some of the overhead allocated to it, like facility costs, wouldn't disappear. Relevant cost analysis for such decisions is in Cost Accounting II.

scenes.q: Under ABC, a product's margin turns negative. What's the best first step?
opts: Check which activities drive its cost and whether they can be reduced or priced
scenes.say: Quick check. Under ABC, a product's margin turns negative. What's the best first step? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B. Understand the activities driving the cost, then price them or reduce them.

videos.title: Value-added and non-value-added activities
videos.take: Eliminate or reduce non-value-added activities that customers don't pay for

scenes.say: Some activities create value customers will pay for. Others just cost money. ABM helps tell them apart.

scenes.heading: Two kinds of activity
scenes.say: A value-added activity is one customers see as worth paying for, like welding a frame or designing a custom layout. A non-value-added activity adds cost but no value, like moving parts around the plant, reworking defects or waiting for setups.

scenes.heading: Cutting setup time
scenes.say: Prairie Gate's two hundred setups take six hours each. With quick-change fixtures, the team thinks they can take three. If the crew and equipment devoted to setups can be cut in half, the setup pool falls from $240,000 to $120,000.

sub: Freed-up time saves money only if
spending falls or capacity is reused
scenes.say: But the savings are real only if spending actually falls, for example by redeploying setup workers, or if the freed capacity is used to build more trailers. Otherwise you have unused capacity, not lower costs.
Cost drivers point straight to the causes of cost, so managers know where to look: fewer setups, fewer defects, fewer engineering changes.

scenes.q: Which activity is non-value-added for Prairie Gate's customers?
opts: Moving steel between storage areas twice
scenes.say: Quick check. Which activity is non-value-added? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's C. Moving steel around adds cost but no value the customer pays for.

videos.title: Design decisions
videos.take: Most costs are locked in at the design stage; ABC shows designers what complexity costs

scenes.say: Most of a product's cost is decided before production starts, when it's designed. ABC tells designers what complexity costs.

sub: Costs not yet incurred but already
scenes.say: Locked-in, or designed-in, costs are costs that haven't been incurred yet but will be, because of decisions already made. Choose a frame with forty unique parts, and the cost of buying, storing and welding them is locked in.

scenes.heading: Livestock trailers: standard designs?
rows: With a menu of 3 standard designs
Setups cut from 160 to 80: per trailer
scenes.say: Today each livestock trailer needs twenty-four design hours. Offering three standard designs with options could cut that to eight, saving sixteen hours at a hundred twenty dollars: $1,920. If setups halve too, that's another $960 a trailer, enough to make the line profitable.
Common parts across models, like the same axles, lights and hitches, cut purchasing, storage and setup activity.

sub: Keep the options customers pay for;
scenes.say: The trade-off: some customers buy from Prairie Gate precisely because of custom design. The goal is to keep the variety customers value and pay for, and drop complexity they don't.

scenes.q: Design hours fall by 10 per trailer at $120 an hour on 100 trailers. Potential saving?
scenes.say: Quick check. Design hours fall by ten per trailer, at a hundred twenty dollars an hour, on a hundred trailers. What's the potential saving? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's C, $120,000, if the design resources are actually reduced.

videos.title: ABC in merchandising and services
videos.take: ABC reveals the cost of serving different customers and services, not just products

scenes.say: A farm supply distributor doesn't make anything. But ABC can still reveal which customers make money.

scenes.heading: Marshall Farm Supply: activity rates
scenes.say: Marshall Farm Supply distributes feed, fencing and parts. Its activity rates: forty dollars to process an order, ninety per delivery, and a hundred fifty extra for each rush order.

scenes.heading: Two customers, same $60,000 of sales a year
scenes.say: Hansen Farms and Berg Dairy each buy $60,000 a year, with the same $12,000 gross margin. Hansen orders monthly: twelve orders and deliveries, no rushes, $1,560 of activity cost. Berg orders small amounts a hundred fifty times, forty of them rushed: $25,500. Berg loses Marshall Farm Supply $13,500 a year.

scenes.heading: What to do about Berg
items: Minimum order sizes or delivery fees
Online ordering to cut processing cost
scenes.say: The answer isn't necessarily to drop Berg. Marshall Farm Supply could set minimum order sizes, charge for deliveries and rush orders, or move Berg to cheaper online ordering.
The same method works in banks, which cost each type of account, hospitals, which cost procedures, and airlines, which cost each fare class.

scenes.q: A customer places 50 orders with 50 deliveries and 10 rushes. Activity cost at $40, $90 and $150?
scenes.say: Quick check. A customer places fifty orders with fifty deliveries and ten rush orders. What's the activity cost? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Time-driven ABC
videos.take: Time-driven ABC uses cost per minute of capacity and minutes per activity

scenes.say: Traditional ABC asks staff how they spend their time. Time-driven ABC replaces the surveys with two simple estimates.

scenes.heading: Two estimates
items: Cost per minute of supplied capacity
scenes.say: Time-driven ABC needs two estimates: the cost per minute of the capacity a department supplies, and the number of minutes each activity takes.

scenes.heading: Prairie Gate's customer service team
scenes.say: Prairie Gate's customer service team costs $560,000 a year. Eight staff each work about seventeen fifty productive hours: eight hundred forty thousand minutes of practical capacity. That's about sixty-seven cents a minute.

scenes.heading: Activity costs
scenes.say: A warranty claim takes thirty minutes: twenty dollars. An order change, fifteen minutes: ten dollars. Setting up a new dealer, four hours: a hundred sixty dollars.
If this year's claims, changes and setups use only seven hundred thousand minutes, a hundred forty thousand minutes, about $93,000 of capacity, is unused. Time-driven ABC makes that visible.

scenes.q: Cost per minute $0.80. An activity takes 45 minutes. Cost?
scenes.say: Quick check. Cost per minute is eighty cents. An activity takes forty-five minutes. What does it cost? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Activity-based budgeting
videos.take: Budget resources from the activities needed to meet planned output

scenes.say: ABC can also run in reverse: start from planned output, work out the activities needed, then budget the resources.

scenes.heading: Activity-based budgeting
scenes.say: Activity-based budgeting starts with the production and sales forecast, estimates the activities needed to deliver it, then the resources those activities require, and finally their cost.

scenes.heading: Prairie Gate, 2028 setups
scenes.say: For 2028, Karen forecasts a hundred fifty setups, thanks to longer utility runs, each taking three hours with the new fixtures. That's four hundred fifty crew hours, so the setup crew can shrink from two people to one, a saving of about $60,000.
Because each budget line is tied to an activity and its driver, managers can see why a cost is there and what would change it.
That ends our work on job costing and ABC. After the midterm, we move to process costing at Redwood Valley Creamery.

scenes.q: Planned 300 inspections at 20 minutes each. How many inspector hours?
scenes.say: Quick check. Three hundred inspections are planned, at twenty minutes each. How many inspector hours? Pause and pick.

warmup: Think of a company that charges extra for things that used to be free: bags on flights, delivery, paper statements. Why?
Those are activity costs that some customers cause. Charging for them is activity-based pricing, an ABM decision.
acts: Using ABC costs, compute each line's total profit at current volumes.
Utility 400 × 500 = $200,000; livestock 100 × −1,880 = −$188,000; total $12,000 before nonmanufacturing costs.
Classify as value-added or non-value-added: welding, rework of bad welds, storing finished trailers for 3 weeks, custom paint, expediting late parts.
Estimate the effect on livestock margin of standard designs (8 design hours) and 80 setups a year, if resources fall proportionately.
Compute customer profit for Olson Ranch: $40,000 sales, 20% margin, 30 orders and deliveries, 5 rushes.
Time-driven ABC: a warehouse costs $300,000 for 500,000 practical minutes. Picking a pallet takes 6 minutes; 60,000 pallets picked. Cost per pallet and unused capacity?
$0.60/min; $3.60 a pallet; used 360,000 min; unused 140,000 min = $84,000.
Prepare an activity-based budget for design if Prairie Gate plans 110 livestock trailers at 8 hours each and 450 utility trailers at 1.5 hours.
case: Karen must decide what to do with the livestock line, which loses $1,880 a trailer under ABC. Engineering proposes three standard designs with 20 options; sales fears losing customers who want fully custom trailers and suggests a $3,000 custom-design fee instead. A consultant suggests dropping the line, noting that $160,000 of the overhead allocated to it is facility-sustaining.
What would each proposal do to the line's margin per trailer?
Why is the consultant's suggestion risky?

Standard designs: about +$2,880 per trailer if resources fall, margin +$1,000. Fee: +$3,000 if customers accept, margin +$1,120. Dropping the line wouldn't remove the $160,000 of facility costs, which would fall on utility trailers, and loses customers who also buy utility trailers. Combine: standard designs as default, fully custom at a fee. Nonfinancial: reputation, loyalty, skilled welders.
exam: Explain activity-based management and give three types of decision it supports.
Using activity cost information to manage: pricing and product mix, cost reduction and process improvement (value-added analysis), design decisions, customer management, budgeting.

Apply ABC to customers in a distributor or service firm

Customers, not just products, drive costs
Cost per minute × minutes per activity

ex.q: A livestock trailer sells for $16,400; DM + DL $8,600; ABC overhead $9,680. Margin per trailer (negative if a loss)?

ex.why: Customers pay for transformation, not for waiting, moving or fixing mistakes.

ex.q: When does cutting setup time actually save money?
opts: Only if resources are reduced or the freed capacity is used
ex.why: Freed time is just unused capacity unless spending falls or output rises.

ex.q: Design hours fall from 24 to 8 per trailer at $120 an hour. Saving per trailer?
Rates: $40 per order, $90 per delivery, $150 per rush. A customer: 20 orders, 20 deliveries, 4 rushes. Activity cost?
A department costs $360,000 a year with 600,000 minutes of practical capacity. What is the cost per minute?
At $0.60 a minute, what does a 50-minute activity cost?

ex.why: Budgeting runs from output to activities to resources.
